overview.goal: Find out where you actually are. No hard running.

gates.label: Pre-participation screening cleared
gates.rationale: The ACSM screening algorithm, applied once before anything else. It exists to catch the small number of people who need clearance -- exertional chest discomfort, unusual breathlessness, exertional dizziness, or known cardiovascular/metabolic/renal disease -- not to put a barrier in front of exercise. Nothing else in this plan runs until it passes, because the plan eventually asks for a maximal effort.

gates.label: Graded ramp test completed
gates.rationale: Everything downstream -- zones, paces, the efficiency baseline -- is derived from it.

gates.label: Structural screen completed
gates.rationale: Finds the specific weak link (usually calf endurance) before load exposes it.

gates.label: At least 7 nights of HRV data
gates.rationale: The readiness engine needs a personal baseline; a population norm is useless here.

overview.goal: Run 30 minutes continuously, comfortably, in Z2.

gates.label: 30 minutes of continuous running
gates.rationale: The classic couch-to-5K endpoint and the precondition for structured aerobic work.

gates.label: That 30 minutes stayed in Z1-Z2
gates.rationale: Running 30 minutes is not the same as running 30 aerobic minutes. If it needed Z4, the aerobic base is not there yet and threshold work would be wasted on you.

gates.label: No pain above 2/10 for two weeks
gates.rationale: The pain-monitoring model treats 0-2/10 as acceptable, 3-5/10 as a warning to hold volume, and anything above 5/10 as a stop. Two clean weeks means the tissue is tolerating the current load, which is the precondition for adding more.

gates.label: 80% of planned sessions completed over 4 weeks
gates.rationale: Consistency is the variable that actually predicts progress. Advancing a phase on the strength of a good fortnight inside a patchy block just moves the problem forward.

overview.goal: Make running a habit and finish a 5K. Volume, not speed.

gates.label: 20+ km/week for three consecutive weeks
gates.rationale: A stable floor of aerobic volume, held long enough to be real rather than a spike.

gates.label: 2000 m time trial completed
gates.rationale: The first honest performance measurement, and 2000 m rather than 5K on purpose. It takes a beginner roughly 11-12 minutes, which sits comfortably inside Riegel's validated 3.5-230 minute window AND inside the range where Daniels' sustainable-%VO2max curve is well behaved. A 5K at this stage is a longer maximal effort on less prepared tissue for a *worse* VDOT estimate. The 5K becomes the next checkpoint, not the first one.

gates.label: 20+ single-leg calf raises per side
gates.rationale: Calf-Achilles endurance is the most common structural limiter in new runners and the one most likely to fail as volume climbs.

gates.label: No pain above 2/10 for two weeks
gates.rationale: The pain-monitoring model treats 0-2/10 as acceptable, 3-5/10 as a warning to hold volume, and anything above 5/10 as a stop. Two clean weeks means the tissue is tolerating the current load, which is the precondition for adding more.

gates.label: 80% of planned sessions completed over 4 weeks
gates.rationale: Consistency is the variable that actually predicts progress. Advancing a phase on the strength of a good fortnight inside a patchy block just moves the problem forward.

overview.goal: Add your first real threshold work and race a 10K.

gates.label: 32+ km/week for three consecutive weeks
gates.rationale: The volume floor that makes threshold work productive instead of merely tiring.

gates.label: A 14 km long run completed
gates.rationale: Roughly a third of the marathon distance -- the checkpoint before half-marathon work.

gates.label: 5K completed continuously
gates.rationale: Recalibrates VDOT over a duration where aerobic endurance starts to show, and the first race-distance checkpoint.

gates.label: Long-run decoupling under 8%
gates.rationale: Heart rate drifting hard relative to pace on a long run means the aerobic base is still thin, whatever the 10K time says. Under 5% is the target; 8% is the gate.

gates.label: No pain above 2/10 for two weeks
gates.rationale: The pain-monitoring model treats 0-2/10 as acceptable, 3-5/10 as a warning to hold volume, and anything above 5/10 as a stop. Two clean weeks means the tissue is tolerating the current load, which is the precondition for adding more.

gates.label: 80% of planned sessions completed over 4 weeks
gates.rationale: Consistency is the variable that actually predicts progress. Advancing a phase on the strength of a good fortnight inside a patchy block just moves the problem forward.

overview.goal: Build the long run and race a half marathon.

gates.label: 42+ km/week for three consecutive weeks
gates.rationale: The base a marathon block is built on. Going into marathon-specific work below this is the single most common reason first marathons go badly.

gates.label: 10K completed
gates.rationale: The first legitimate Riegel input. Below 10K the extrapolation to marathon distance spans too large a distance ratio to mean much, which is why no marathon prediction appears before this.

gates.label: A 20 km long run completed
gates.rationale: Half-marathon readiness.

gates.label: Half marathon completed
gates.rationale: The best available predictor of marathon readiness, and a rehearsal of fuelling, pacing and kit at a distance where mistakes are survivable.

gates.label: No pain above 2/10 for two weeks
gates.rationale: The pain-monitoring model treats 0-2/10 as acceptable, 3-5/10 as a warning to hold volume, and anything above 5/10 as a stop. Two clean weeks means the tissue is tolerating the current load, which is the precondition for adding more.

gates.label: 80% of planned sessions completed over 4 weeks
gates.rationale: Consistency is the variable that actually predicts progress. Advancing a phase on the strength of a good fortnight inside a patchy block just moves the problem forward.

overview.goal: Develop marathon-specific endurance: the long run is the point.

gates.label: Three long runs of 26 km or more
gates.rationale: Time on feet is the specific adaptation the marathon demands, and one long run does not build it.

gates.label: Long-run decoupling under 6%
gates.rationale: Aerobic durability at duration -- the thing that decides whether the last 10 km is running or survival.

gates.label: 48+ km/week for three consecutive weeks
gates.rationale: Peak-phase volume floor for a 3-day-a-week schedule with cross-training.

gates.label: No pain above 2/10 for two weeks
gates.rationale: The pain-monitoring model treats 0-2/10 as acceptable, 3-5/10 as a warning to hold volume, and anything above 5/10 as a stop. Two clean weeks means the tissue is tolerating the current load, which is the precondition for adding more.

gates.label: 80% of planned sessions completed over 4 weeks
gates.rationale: Consistency is the variable that actually predicts progress. Advancing a phase on the strength of a good fortnight inside a patchy block just moves the problem forward.

overview.goal: Rehearse race day -- marathon pace, fuelling, and the long run at size.

gates.label: Two long runs with marathon-pace segments
gates.rationale: Rehearses race pace on tired legs, which is the only way to know it is realistic.

gates.label: A long run of 150+ minutes
gates.rationale: Time on feet matters more than distance for a first marathon.

gates.label: Race fuelling rehearsed on two long runs
gates.rationale: The gut is trainable and untrained guts fail at 30 km. Practise the exact products and timing you will use.

gates.label: No pain above 2/10 for two weeks
gates.rationale: The pain-monitoring model treats 0-2/10 as acceptable, 3-5/10 as a warning to hold volume, and anything above 5/10 as a stop. Two clean weeks means the tissue is tolerating the current load, which is the precondition for adding more.

weeks.focus: Find out where you actually are. No hard running.
notes: No hard running this week, on purpose. A maximal test on untrained tissue measures discomfort tolerance and buys an injury.
Wear the armband overnight every night from now on -- the readiness engine needs at least 14 nights before its band means anything.

sessions.title: Screening + baseline day -- no running
sessions.intent: Two things, in this order. First the pre-participation screening questionnaire -- it takes two minutes and gates everything else. Then the orthostatic test on waking (5 min supine, 2 min standing) and the start of the overnight HRV series. No running today.
cues: The screening is not a formality: exertional chest discomfort, unusual breathlessness and exertional dizziness are the three answers that stop the plan, and they stop it whether or not you feel like they should.
Wear the armband tonight in resting mode so the HRV baseline starts building immediately -- it needs 14 nights before it means anything.

sessions.title: Structural screen
sessions.structure: Single-leg calf raises to failure per side; 30 s sit-to-stand; single-leg balance; step-down quality; plank hold.
sessions.intent: Find the weak link before load finds it.

sessions.title: Graded ramp test
sessions.structure: 5 min walk warm-up, then 4 min stages at 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 km/h. Record heart rate over the final 60 s of each stage, plus Borg 6-20 and the talk test. Stop at 85% of heart-rate reserve, RPE 15/20, or when speech becomes impossible.
sessions.intent: Derive the heart-rate/speed relationship, the talk-test threshold, cadence at each speed, and the seed VDOT. Everything else follows.

sessions.title: Rest
sessions.intent: Recover from the ramp.

sessions.title: Easy shakeout walk-jog
sessions.intent: Confirm the sensor setup and the audio cues work before anything depends on them.

sessions.intent: Adaptation happens now, not during the session.

phases.goal: Run 30 minutes continuously, comfortably, in Z2.

gates.label: 30 minutes of continuous running
gates.rationale: The classic couch-to-5K endpoint and the precondition for structured aerobic work.

gates.label: That 30 minutes stayed in Z1-Z2
gates.rationale: Running 30 minutes is not the same as running 30 aerobic minutes. If it needed Z4, the aerobic base is not there yet and threshold work would be wasted on you.

gates.label: No pain above 2/10 for two weeks
gates.rationale: The pain-monitoring model treats 0-2/10 as acceptable, 3-5/10 as a warning to hold volume, and anything above 5/10 as a stop. Two clean weeks means the tissue is tolerating the current load, which is the precondition for adding more.

weeks.focus: Run 30 minutes continuously, comfortably, in Z2.
notes: Run-walk ladder rung 1 of 8: 1 min running / 2 min walking x 8 (8 min of running per session, 24 min across the week).
Repeat a rung rather than advancing if the previous week felt hard, hurt, or was interrupted. There is no deadline.

sessions.title: Strength (running-specific)
sessions.structure: Heavy slow calf raises: 3 x 12 straight-knee + 3 x 12 bent-knee, 3 s down. Add load once 12 reps is easy -- this is the single highest-yield injury-prevention exercise for a runner.; Single-leg work: split squats or step-ups, 3 x 8 per side, loaded.; Hip abduction: side-lying or cable, 3 x 15 per side.; Posterior chain: Romanian deadlift or hip thrust, 3 x 8.; Anti-rotation core: Pallof press or suitcase carry, 3 x 30 s per side.
sessions.intent: Injury prevention and running economy. Strength training substantially reduces overuse injury (Lauersen 2014/2018) and improves running economy without unwanted mass (Blagrove 2018). You already lift -- fold these in rather than adding a separate session.
cues: Keep heavy lower-body work at least 24 h away from a quality run and 48 h from the long run.
Do not chase soreness. The goal is stiffness and strength, not a session that compromises the running.

sessions.title: Rest
sessions.intent: Adaptation happens now, not during the session.

sessions.title: Run-walk 1/2 x 8
sessions.structure: 5 min walk warm-up, then 8 x (1 min easy running + 2 min walking), 5 min walk cool-down.
sessions.intent: Build running-specific tissue tolerance in doses the tissue can actually absorb. The walk break is not a concession -- it is what keeps the running portions aerobic and the total load survivable.
cues: Run the running portions slowly enough that the walk break feels almost unnecessary.
Do not skip the walk breaks because you feel good. The breaks are why you feel good.

Add load once 12 reps is easy -- this is the single highest-yield injury-prevention exercise for a runner.; Single-leg work: split squats or step-ups, 3 x 8 per side, loaded.; Hip abduction: side-lying or cable, 3 x 15 per side.; Posterior chain: Romanian deadlift or hip thrust, 3 x 8.; Anti-rotation core: Pallof press or suitcase carry, 3 x 30 s per side.
sessions.intent: Injury prevention and running economy. Strength training substantially reduces overuse injury (Lauersen 2014/2018) and improves running economy without unwanted mass (Blagrove 2018). You already lift -- fold these in rather than adding a separate session.
cues: Keep heavy lower-body work at least 24 h away from a quality run and 48 h from the long run.
Do not chase soreness. The goal is stiffness and strength, not a session that compromises the running.

phases.goal: Make running a habit and finish a 5K. Volume, not speed.

gates.label: 20+ km/week for three consecutive weeks
gates.rationale: A stable floor of aerobic volume, held long enough to be real rather than a spike.

gates.label: 2000 m time trial completed
gates.rationale: The first honest performance measurement, and 2000 m rather than 5K on purpose. It takes a beginner roughly 11-12 minutes, which sits comfortably inside Riegel's validated 3.5-230 minute window AND inside the range where Daniels' sustainable-%VO2max curve is well behaved. A 5K at this stage is a longer maximal effort on less prepared tissue for a *worse* VDOT estimate. The 5K becomes the next checkpoint, not the first one.

gates.label: 20+ single-leg calf raises per side
gates.rationale: Calf-Achilles endurance is the most common structural limiter in new runners and the one most likely to fail as volume climbs.

gates.label: No pain above 2/10 for two weeks
gates.rationale: The pain-monitoring model treats 0-2/10 as acceptable, 3-5/10 as a warning to hold volume, and anything above 5/10 as a stop. Two clean weeks means the tissue is tolerating the current load, which is the precondition for adding more.

gates.label: 80% of planned sessions completed over 4 weeks
gates.rationale: Consistency is the variable that actually predicts progress. Advancing a phase on the strength of a good fortnight inside a patchy block just moves the problem forward.

weeks.focus: Make running a habit and finish a 5K. Volume, not speed.
notes: Daniels would cap the long run at 30% of weekly volume at this level; this one is 35%. Three runs a week leaves no other way to build a marathon long run, so this is a real and accepted trade-off rather than an oversight -- and the time cap is what keeps it bounded.
No threshold work yet. Volume and consistency first -- threshold work on a thin base produces fatigue without much adaptation.

sessions.title: Long run
sessions.structure: Steady and easy throughout.
sessions.intent: Time on feet. This is the session the marathon is actually built from -- mitochondrial and capillary density, fat oxidation, tendon and bone tolerance, and the confidence that comes from having been out there.

Start slower than feels natural. Negative-split the run if you can.
Decoupling is the metric that matters here: if heart rate drifts more than 5% relative to pace between the halves, the pace was too hot for the duration.

sessions.intent: Aerobic development with minimal cost. This is the session most often ruined by running it too fast.
cues: If you cannot hold a conversation, you are going too fast -- slow down, do not shorten it.
Heart rate is the referee, not pace. On a hot day or a bad-sleep day the same effort is a slower pace, and that is correct, not a setback.
Strides should feel fast and easy, never strained. Stop the set if form degrades.

sessions.title: Long run
sessions.structure: Steady and easy throughout.
sessions.intent: Time on feet. This is the session the marathon is actually built from -- mitochondrial and capillary density, fat oxidation, tendon and bone tolerance, and the confidence that comes from having been out there.
cues: Daniels would cap the long run at 30% of weekly volume at this level; this one is 50%. Three runs a week leaves no other way to build a marathon long run, so this is a real and accepted trade-off rather than an oversight -- and the time cap is what keeps it bounded.
The long run is 50% of your week. That is high, and it is the unavoidable cost of a 3-run week -- the textbook figure is 30-35%. Adding a short fourth easy run is the cleanest way to bring it down.
Start slower than feels natural. Negative-split the run if you can.
Decoupling is the metric that matters here: if heart rate drifts more than 5% relative to pace between the halves, the pace was too hot for the duration.
sessions.fuelling: Take 30-60 g of carbohydrate per hour after the first hour, and drink to thirst. Above ~2.5 h aim toward 60-90 g/h using a glucose+fructose mix -- the gut is trainable and this is the training (ACSM/ISSN guidance; the high end needs practice, so build up to it rather than trying it on race day).

sessions.title: Strength (running-specific)
sessions.structure: Heavy slow calf raises: 3 x 12 straight-knee + 3 x 12 bent-knee, 3 s down. Add load once 12 reps is easy -- this is the single highest-yield injury-prevention exercise for a runner.; Single-leg work: split squats or step-ups, 3 x 8 per side, loaded.; Hip abduction: side-lying or cable, 3 x 15 per side.; Posterior chain: Romanian deadlift or hip thrust, 3 x 8.; Anti-rotation core: Pallof press or suitcase carry, 3 x 30 s per side.; Low-amplitude plyometrics: 3 x 10 pogo hops, 2 x 10 alternating bounds. Stiffness work -- improves running economy (Blagrove 2018); introduce only once the calf-raise gate is met, and never within 48 h of a long run.

cues: Keep heavy lower-body work at least 24 h away from a quality run and 48 h from the long run.
Do not chase soreness. The goal is stiffness and strength, not a session that compromises the running.

phases.goal: Add your first real threshold work and race a 10K.

gates.label: 32+ km/week for three consecutive weeks
gates.rationale: The volume floor that makes threshold work productive instead of merely tiring.

gates.label: A 14 km long run completed
gates.rationale: Roughly a third of the marathon distance -- the checkpoint before half-marathon work.

gates.label: 5K completed continuously
gates.rationale: Recalibrates VDOT over a duration where aerobic endurance starts to show, and the first race-distance checkpoint.

gates.label: Long-run decoupling under 8%
gates.rationale: Heart rate drifting hard relative to pace on a long run means the aerobic base is still thin, whatever the 10K time says. Under 5% is the target; 8% is the gate.

gates.label: No pain above 2/10 for two weeks
gates.rationale: The pain-monitoring model treats 0-2/10 as acceptable, 3-5/10 as a warning to hold volume, and anything above 5/10 as a stop. Two clean weeks means the tissue is tolerating the current load, which is the precondition for adding more.

gates.label: 80% of planned sessions completed over 4 weeks
gates.rationale: Consistency is the variable that actually predicts progress. Advancing a phase on the strength of a good fortnight inside a patchy block just moves the problem forward.

gates.label: 42+ km/week for three consecutive weeks
gates.rationale: The base a marathon block is built on. Going into marathon-specific work below this is the single most common reason first marathons go badly.

gates.label: 10K completed
gates.rationale: The first legitimate Riegel input. Below 10K the extrapolation to marathon distance spans too large a distance ratio to mean much, which is why no marathon prediction appears before this.

gates.label: A 20 km long run completed
gates.rationale: Half-marathon readiness.

gates.label: Half marathon completed
gates.rationale: The best available predictor of marathon readiness, and a rehearsal of fuelling, pacing and kit at a distance where mistakes are survivable.

gates.label: No pain above 2/10 for two weeks
gates.rationale: The pain-monitoring model treats 0-2/10 as acceptable, 3-5/10 as a warning to hold volume, and anything above 5/10 as a stop. Two clean weeks means the tissue is tolerating the current load, which is the precondition for adding more.

gates.label: 80% of planned sessions completed over 4 weeks
gates.rationale: Consistency is the variable that actually predicts progress. Advancing a phase on the strength of a good fortnight inside a patchy block just moves the problem forward.

Add load once 12 reps is easy -- this is the single highest-yield injury-prevention exercise for a runner.; Single-leg work: split squats or step-ups, 3 x 8 per side, loaded.; Hip abduction: side-lying or cable, 3 x 15 per side.; Posterior chain: Romanian deadlift or hip thrust, 3 x 8.; Anti-rotation core: Pallof press or suitcase carry, 3 x 30 s per side.; Low-amplitude plyometrics: 3 x 10 pogo hops, 2 x 10 alternating bounds. Stiffness work -- improves running economy (Blagrove 2018); introduce only once the calf-raise gate is met, and never within 48 h of a long run.
sessions.intent: Injury prevention and running economy. Strength training substantially reduces overuse injury (Lauersen 2014/2018) and improves running economy without unwanted mass (Blagrove 2018). You already lift -- fold these in rather than adding a separate session.
cues: Keep heavy lower-body work at least 24 h away from a quality run and 48 h from the long run.
Do not chase soreness. The goal is stiffness and strength, not a session that compromises the running.

sessions.title: Rest
sessions.intent: Adaptation happens now, not during the session.

sessions.title: Threshold 3 x 8 min
sessions.structure: 20 min easy warm-up, then 3 x 8 min at threshold pace (8:03/km) with 2 min easy jog between, then 10 min easy cool-down.

cues: Threshold is 'comfortably hard' -- about the pace you could hold for an hour in a race. If rep 1 feels hard, it is too fast.
Heart rate lags: expect it to reach the zone about 90 seconds into each rep. Do not chase the number at the start of the rep.

sessions.title: Long run
sessions.structure: Steady and easy throughout.
sessions.intent: Time on feet. This is the session the marathon is actually built from -- mitochondrial and capillary density, fat oxidation, tendon and bone tolerance, and the confidence that comes from having been out there.

sessions.title: Threshold 5 x 10 min
sessions.structure: 20 min easy warm-up, then 5 x 10 min at threshold pace (8:03/km) with 2 min easy jog between, then 10 min easy cool-down.
sessions.intent: Raise the pace you can hold for an hour. Cruise intervals rather than one long tempo because broken threshold work accumulates more time at the intensity for less fatigue -- Daniels' own argument for the format.

cues: Threshold is 'comfortably hard' -- about the pace you could hold for an hour in a race. If rep 1 feels hard, it is too fast.
Heart rate lags: expect it to reach the zone about 90 seconds into each rep. Do not chase the number at the start of the rep.

sessions.title: Strength (running-specific)
sessions.structure: Heavy slow calf raises: 3 x 12 straight-knee + 3 x 12 bent-knee, 3 s down. Add load once 12 reps is easy -- this is the single highest-yield injury-prevention exercise for a runner.; Single-leg work: split squats or step-ups, 3 x 8 per side, loaded.; Hip abduction: side-lying or cable, 3 x 15 per side.; Posterior chain: Romanian deadlift or hip thrust, 3 x 8.; Anti-rotation core: Pallof press or suitcase carry, 3 x 30 s per side.; Low-amplitude plyometrics: 3 x 10 pogo hops, 2 x 10 alternating bounds. Stiffness work -- improves running economy (Blagrove 2018); introduce only once the calf-raise gate is met, and never within 48 h of a long run.
sessions.intent: Injury prevention and running economy. Strength training substantially reduces overuse injury (Lauersen 2014/2018) and improves running economy without unwanted mass (Blagrove 2018). You already lift -- fold these in rather than adding a separate session.
cues: Keep heavy lower-body work at least 24 h away from a quality run and 48 h from the long run.
Do not chase soreness. The goal is stiffness and strength, not a session that compromises the running.

sessions.intent: Aerobic development with minimal cost. This is the session most often ruined by running it too fast.

Heart rate is the referee, not pace. On a hot day or a bad-sleep day the same effort is a slower pace, and that is correct, not a setback.

sessions.title: Long run
sessions.structure: Steady easy running; see the marathon-pace weeks for segment work.
sessions.intent: Time on feet. This is the session the marathon is actually built from -- mitochondrial and capillary density, fat oxidation, tendon and bone tolerance, and the confidence that comes from having been out there.
cues: Short by design. You cannot gain fitness now; you can only arrive tired.
Start slower than feels natural. Negative-split the run if you can.
Decoupling is the metric that matters here: if heart rate drifts more than 5% relative to pace between the halves, the pace was too hot for the duration.

weeks.focus: Cut volume, keep intensity, arrive fresh.
notes: Bosquet 2007 meta-analysis: a 2-week taper with a 41-60% volume reduction, holding intensity and frequency, produced the largest performance gain. Cutting intensity instead of volume is what makes people feel flat on race day.
Volume is 30% of peak. Intensity and frequency stay.

keep: intensity -- the quality session stays at threshold/MP pace, just shorter
taper.rationale: Bosquet 2007 meta-analysis: a 2-week taper with a 41-60% volume reduction, holding intensity and frequency, produced the largest performance gain. Cutting intensity instead of volume is what makes people feel flat on race day.

caveats: Seed VDOT is 22, below the floor of Daniels' published tables (~30), so the VDOT pace formulas extrapolate to paces slower than a brisk walk. They are therefore NOT being used yet: your prescribed paces come from the heart-rate/speed relationship measured in your own ramp test. That is a better instrument for you right now, and the plan switches to VDOT automatically once a real time trial puts you above 30.
Seed VDOT comes from a SUBMAXIMAL test and is deliberately conservative -- expect it to rise sharply at the week-4 time trial. Do not chase the early paces.
HRmax is an age-based estimate with roughly +/-7 bpm standard error and up to 20 bpm individual error. Zones will be re-anchored after the first hard time trial.
Marathon prediction uses a novice-adjusted Riegel exponent (1.15, not 1.06) because low-mileage first-timers fade much harder over the last 12 km than the standard formula assumes.
The HR-speed fit was measured between 5 and 9 km/h. Any prescribed pace faster than that is an extrapolation -- the plan does not prescribe outside it during the foundation phase.
